body:
Why is cybersecurity necessary?

Computers, smartphones and the Internet have become essential for communication, banking, education, healthcare, commerce and public administration. Citizens use digital services to make payments, obtain certificates, submit applications and access government records. Public institutions use computer systems to store information and deliver services.

These activities create a need to protect digital devices, information, accounts and services against unauthorised access, manipulation, disruption and fraud.

Cybersecurity

Cybersecurity is the protection of computers, digital devices, networks, software and electronic information against cyber threats. It includes measures to prevent incidents, detect suspicious activity, limit damage and restore affected services.

Cybersecurity and information security

Information security protects information against unauthorised access, disclosure, alteration, destruction and disruption, regardless of whether that information is stored digitally or physically. Cybersecurity focuses on threats involving digital systems, networks and electronic information.

For example, preventing unauthorised access to a government database is a cybersecurity measure. Protecting a confidential paper register in a locked cabinet is an information security measure. Both protect information, but only the first necessarily involves a digital system.

The 3 basic goals of information security

Information security is commonly explained through Confidentiality, Integrity and Availability, collectively called the CIA triad.

  • Confidentiality: Information should be accessible only to authorised persons. If an outsider obtains citizens' private records without permission, confidentiality is compromised.
  • Integrity: Information should remain accurate and should not be changed without authorisation. If an unauthorised person alters a beneficiary's bank account details, integrity is compromised.
  • Availability: Authorised users should be able to access information and services when needed. If malicious software makes a public-service portal unusable, availability is compromised.

A single incident may affect more than 1 goal. For example, malware may steal confidential records, alter files and interrupt services.

Threat, vulnerability, control and incident

These terms describe different parts of a security problem.

  • Threat: A possible source of harm, such as malware, a fraudulent message or an unauthorised user.
  • Vulnerability: A weakness that may allow harm to occur, such as outdated software or an easily guessed password.
  • Security control: A measure that reduces risk, such as installing updates, requiring authentication or restricting access.
  • Security incident: An event that actually or potentially compromises the security of information or systems.

Example from public administration

A district office maintains a digital database of beneficiaries. An attacker is a potential threat. An unprotected administrative account is a vulnerability. Strong authentication and restricted permissions are controls. Unauthorised modification of beneficiary records is a security incident.

A threat does not automatically produce an incident. Harm depends on circumstances, weaknesses and the effectiveness of protective measures.

Why this distinction matters

Different threats require different controls. A firewall controls certain network connections, while authentication helps verify identity. Neither necessarily prevents a person from voluntarily disclosing a banking PIN to a fraudster. Effective cybersecurity therefore combines technical safeguards, safe user behaviour and institutional procedures.

Prelims focus

  • Information security protects information in both physical and digital forms.
  • Cybersecurity focuses on digital systems, networks and information.
  • CIA stands for Confidentiality, Integrity and Availability.
  • A vulnerability is a weakness; a threat is a potential source of harm.
  • A security control reduces risk but does not necessarily eliminate it.
  • Trap: Availability means access to information or services when needed, not unrestricted public access.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Environment, Class 7, Chapter 7, Human Environment: Settlement, Transport and Communication, printed p. 52, 2018-19 edition; NCERT, Fundamentals of Human Geography, Class 12, Chapter 8, Transport and Communication, section Cyber Space: Internet, printed p. 79; National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST), Small Business Cybersecurity Glossary, entries Information Security, Cybersecurity, Confidentiality, Integrity, Availability and Cyber Incident, updated 9 April 2025; online sources consulted 16 November 2026.]

title: Cybersecurity and Information Security: Meaning, Scope and Basic Concepts

body:
What is malware?

Malware is the shortened form of malicious software. It refers to software intentionally designed or used to compromise a device, information or computer system.

Malware may steal information, modify or destroy files, interfere with normal operations, secretly monitor users or provide unauthorised access to a system. The harm depends on the type of malware and the privileges it obtains.

Malware can affect computers, smartphones and other digital devices. It may be encountered through suspicious attachments, deceptive downloads, untrusted applications, infected removable media or compromised software.

Major types of malware

1. Computer virus

A computer virus is malicious code that attaches itself to another file or program and can reproduce when the infected host is executed. Its propagation generally depends on the infected file or program being run or shared.

A virus may modify or damage files, interfere with software or perform other malicious activities.

2. Computer worm

A worm is malware that can reproduce and spread between computers or systems without attaching itself to a legitimate host file in the same way as a conventional virus.

Unlike a virus, a worm is generally a standalone malicious program. Worms may spread automatically under suitable conditions and can affect multiple connected systems.

Virus and worm

A virus typically reproduces by infecting a host file or program. A worm can reproduce as an independent program and spread between systems. Both are malware, but their methods of propagation differ.

3. Trojan horse

A Trojan horse, or Trojan, is malicious software presented as a legitimate or useful program. Its deceptive appearance encourages a user to install or execute it.

Once installed, a Trojan may steal information, interfere with the device or permit unauthorised remote access. Some Trojans create a backdoor, meaning a concealed means of accessing a system without following its normal access restrictions.

A Trojan is distinguished by its deceptive presentation. Unlike viruses and worms, self-replication is not its defining characteristic.

4. Spyware

Spyware secretly gathers information about a user or device. It may monitor activities or collect sensitive details without the user's informed permission.

Spyware primarily threatens confidentiality, although its presence may also create other security risks.

5. Ransomware

Ransomware is malware that denies access to data or systems and demands payment. It commonly makes files unusable through unauthorised encryption. Its defining feature is the use of restricted access or threatened harm to demand a ransom.

Ransomware is examined separately because it creates a particularly important risk to the availability of information and services.

Malware and phishing are not the same

Malware is malicious software. Phishing is a deceptive communication intended to trick someone into revealing information or taking an unsafe action.

A fraudulent email may ask a person to disclose a password without installing any malware. Alternatively, a phishing message may contain a harmful attachment that installs malware. Therefore, phishing and malware are distinct concepts, although they can occur together.

Basic protection against malware

  • Install applications from trusted, official sources.
  • Keep operating systems, browsers and applications updated.
  • Use reputable anti-malware protection and keep it updated.
  • Avoid opening unexpected attachments or running untrusted files.
  • Maintain separate recoverable backups of important information.
  • Report suspected infection of an official device to the responsible IT or security team.

Anti-malware software can detect and block many threats, but no product guarantees detection of every malicious program. User caution and regular maintenance remain necessary.

Prelims focus

  • Malware is an umbrella term covering several types of malicious software.
  • A virus typically attaches to a host file or program.
  • A worm can reproduce and spread as an independent program.
  • A Trojan disguises itself as legitimate software and may create a backdoor.
  • Spyware secretly collects information; ransomware restricts access and demands payment.
  • Trap: Every virus is malware, but not every malware program is a virus.

[Sources: NIST, Small Business Cybersecurity Glossary, entries Malware, Spyware, Ransomware and Antivirus/Anti-malware Software, updated 9 April 2025; Government of India, National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal, Cyber Crime Categories, sections Virus, Worms and Trojans and Ransomware; CERT-In, Advisory CIAD-2025-0019, Essential Measures for Industry for Safeguarding Business Operations against Cyber Security Threats, issued 10 May 2025; Gujarat Public Service Commission, Provisional Answer Key, Advertisement 47/2023-24, Preliminary Test held 7 January 2024, Paper 2, Question 121, printed p. 49, published 10 January 2024; online sources consulted 16 November 2026.]

title: Malware: Meaning, Common Types and Their Differences

body:
How ransomware differs from other malware

Ransomware is a type of malware associated with extortion. The attacker makes data or a system inaccessible and demands payment in exchange for a claimed restoration of access.

Many ransomware incidents involve the malicious encryption of files, making them unreadable without the necessary decryption information. Some ransomware instead locks access to the device or service.

Ransomware can affect individuals, businesses and public institutions. Its impact may include loss of access to important records, interruption of services, recovery costs and possible exposure of information.

What happens in a typical ransomware incident?

  1. Compromise: Malware reaches a vulnerable or inadequately protected device or system.
  2. Restriction of access: The malware makes selected files or services inaccessible, commonly through encryption.
  3. Ransom demand: The attacker demands payment and claims that access will be restored.
  4. Service disruption: The affected user or institution may be unable to continue normal activities until the problem is safely resolved.

This is a general description of the consequences, not a necessary sequence for every ransomware incident. The exact effects depend on the malware and the affected system.

Why backups are important

A backup is a separate copy of information maintained so that data can be recovered if the original becomes lost, corrupted or inaccessible.

Backups are especially valuable against ransomware because an unaffected, usable copy of important files may support recovery without relying on an attacker's promise.

However, a backup provides protection only if it remains available and can actually be restored. A backup continuously accessible from a compromised system may itself be damaged. For this reason, important backups should be stored separately or appropriately isolated, and restoration should be checked periodically.

Prevention and response

Ransomware protection combines several controls rather than relying on a single application.

  • Software updates: Reduce exposure to known software weaknesses that malware may exploit.
  • Anti-malware protection: Helps identify and block malicious software.
  • Strong authentication: Makes unauthorised account access more difficult.
  • Access restrictions: Limit what a compromised user account may change.
  • Separate backups: Support restoration of affected information.
  • User awareness: Reduces the likelihood of opening suspicious files or installing untrusted applications.

Payment does not guarantee recovery

Paying a ransom does not guarantee that files will be restored or that stolen information will remain confidential. Affected public institutions should follow their authorised incident-reporting and recovery procedures rather than independently negotiating with attackers.

If ransomware is suspected, a citizen should avoid further interaction with the suspicious software and seek reliable assistance. A government employee should promptly notify the designated IT or cybersecurity team so that the incident can be handled without unnecessarily disturbing potential evidence.

Application to public systems

Suppose a district hospital stores appointment schedules and patient records digitally. Ransomware may prevent authorised medical staff from accessing these records. This illustrates a failure of availability. If confidential records are also disclosed without permission, confidentiality is additionally affected.

The distinction matters because restoring access and preventing unauthorised disclosure are related but different security objectives.

Prelims focus

  • Ransomware is a type of malware.
  • It commonly restricts access to data through malicious encryption.
  • A ransomware attack can compromise availability and may affect confidentiality.
  • Separate, restorable backups reduce dependence on ransom-based recovery.
  • Software updates, anti-malware protection and access restrictions help reduce risk.
  • Trap: A backup assists recovery; it does not necessarily prevent the initial infection.

[Sources: NIST, Small Business Cybersecurity Glossary, entries Ransomware, Backups, Availability and Cyber Incident, updated 9 April 2025; CERT-In, Advisory CIAD-2025-0019, sections Patch Management, Secure Network and Endpoint Devices, Implement Robust Data Protection Strategies and Develop an Incident Response Plan, issued 10 May 2025; online sources consulted 16 November 2026.]
